newsitem.title: PERU: Peru set for hostage talks, but asylum off agenda.
newsitem.headline: Peru set for hostage talks, but asylum off agenda.

text.p: Peru's government and Marxist rebels were poised to return to the negotiating table on Wednesday -- but an asylum offer from Cuba was apparently off the agenda as the Lima hostage crisis dragged into its 78th day.

Both sides were scheduled to meet for a ninth round of talks in a safe house opposite the besieged Japanese ambassador's residence, where some 20 Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels were holding 72 hostages.
President Alberto Fujimori said on the eve of the talks that his government was preparing an "all-inclusive proposal" to end without bloodshed Latin America's longest hostage siege
But the president gave no details of the proposal, which his negotiator, Domingo Palermo, was expected to present to the MRTA at the new meeting.
Fujimori was speaking after the rebels rejected an asylum offer he brokered with Cuban leader Fidel Castro during a surprise visit to the Caribbean nation.
He added that Peru would not give up either its search for a bloodless end to the siege or its stance against bowing to the MRTA demand for the release of some 400 jailed comrades.

Pouring cold water on government optimism over the Cuba option, MRTA leader Nestor Cerpa insisted on Tuesday in a walkie-talkie conversation monitored by Reuters that the rebels wanted to stay in Peru.

Speaking from his stronghold within the captured Japanese ambassador's Lima residence, Cerpa added that the eight rounds of talks so far have only led to both sides entrenching themselves behind their initial positions.
"We believe this (the talks) cannot continue indefinitely in the sense that they can get worn down and lose a certain level of legitimacy," he warned.
Cerpa added that the stalemate led him to decide not to attend the eighth round of talks on Monday, sending his deputy, Rolly Rojas. It was not known who would attend on Wednesday for the MRTA.
On the other side of the bargaining table, Fujimori held his position.
"There has been no proposal for an amnesty (for rebels) presented to Congress and no proposal for an amnesty for the MRTA prisoners," he said in the southern city of Arequipa.
Fujimori has hinted at other concessions, possibly including a softening of the harsh conditions for MRTA prisoners and a reform of trial processes.
But the rebels have repeatedly insisted -- and now chant daily during their morning exercise routines -- that they will not surrender for anything less than releases of comrades.
The MRTA repeated that demand, and slammed Fujimori's "dictatorship" for "atrocious" jail conditions, in a statement sent to Reuters via e-mail early on Wednesday.

The statement, from the MRTA's international spokesman, Isaac Velazco, criticised "the toughening of jail conditions, the suspension of the 30-minute visits once a month, the lack of medical attention, the denial of entry for the Red Cross, the physical and psychological tortures."

The MRTA sought a "political and peaceful solution" to the crisis, but talks were stretching out because the government was distracted by an attempt to "justify itself and and look for those responsible for negligence" in the Dec. 17 raid, the statement added.

The rebels initially seized more than 500 captives at a cocktail party to celebrate the Japanese Emperor's birthday. The remaining hostages include Fujimori's brother, Pedro, two government ministers, the envoys of Japan and Bolivia, and two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen.
